prohibited_recommendations: Do not commit the patient to cervical spine surgery on the basis of incidental spondylotic changes when EMG findings extend beyond the cervical cord.
Do not start chronic immunosuppression (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange) for ALS — there is no benefit and treatment delays correct diagnosis.
Do not defer respiratory assessment in a symptomatic patient — even mild FVC reduction warrants close monitoring and NIV planning.
Do not dismiss bulbar or progressive symptoms as functional / psychiatric without a complete neurological workup.
Do not continue oral feeding without a swallowing assessment given documented dysphagia and aspiration risk.
required_recommendations: Perform EMG/NCS sampling the bulbar region plus ≥2 spinal regions to document lower-motor-neuron involvement and exclude conduction block.
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural mimics (cervical myelopathy, demyelinating disease, brainstem tumor).
Order a mimic-exclusion lab panel (CK, B12, TSH, HIV, RPR, SPEP, anti-GM1 IgM, androgen receptor CAG repeat in males).
Measure baseline respiratory function (FVC, MIP/MEP, SNIP) to inform NIV timing.
Obtain a swallowing evaluation by speech-language pathology given dysphagia and aspiration risk.
Apply Awaji-Shima 2008 / Gold Coast 2020 criteria to confirm the diagnosis.
Initiate riluzole 50 mg twice daily after baseline LFTs unless contraindicated; arrange monthly LFT monitoring for the first 3 months.
Refer to a multidisciplinary ALS clinic for SLP, dietetics, respiratory, and social-work input.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

differential.key_features: Multilevel cervical spondylosis with C5-C6 stenosis on MRI, but cord signal preserved and findings above C3 (bulbar) are unexplained
Bulbar-onset presentation; EMG shows widespread involvement beyond bulbar, consistent with bulbar-onset ALS rather than restricted PBP

differential.diagnosis: Multifocal motor neuropathy (MMN) with conduction block
differential.key_features: No conduction block on motor NCS; anti-GM1 negative; bulbar involvement atypical
No fatigable weakness or ocular signs; EMG shows denervation rather than decrement
Female sex makes X-linked SBMA essentially impossible; androgen receptor CAG repeat normal

key_clinical_evidence: Diagnosis requires evidence of both upper-motor-neuron involvement (hyperreflexia, Babinski, Hoffman, brisk jaw jerk, spasticity) and lower-motor-neuron involvement (atrophy, fasciculations, EMG denervation) with progressive spread, while excluding mimics — Awaji 2008 / Gold Coast 2020.

EMG in bulbar plus ≥2 spinal regions documenting fibrillations, positive sharp waves, complex fasciculation potentials, and large-amplitude long-duration polyphasic MUPs with reduced recruitment satisfies the electrodiagnostic criterion.
Normal sensory NCS and absence of conduction block are pivotal: they exclude common mimics including multifocal motor neuropathy, CIDP, and Kennedy disease.
Mild-to-moderate CK elevation (2–5× ULN) is consistent with ALS and does not itself indicate a primary myopathy.
Cervical spondylotic changes on MRI are common incidental findings in the at-risk age group; bulbar findings or multi-region EMG denervation cannot be attributed to cervical disease.
Baseline FVC, MIP/MEP, and SNIP/NIF inform NIV timing — NIV initiation at FVC <50% predicted or SNIP <40 cmH₂O prolongs survival and improves quality of life.
Bulbar-onset disease carries a worse prognosis; early NIV planning and swallowing/feeding strategy are higher priority than in limb-onset disease.

July 2026 review applied end to end: EMG/NCS is the required ALS-specific test; brain and cord MRI and targeted labs exclude mimics; respiratory function is a recommended safety baseline; genetics is separately offered after counselling; CSF is absent except in five atypical mimic work-ups.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillations +2, fasciculation potentials with complex morphology. Motor unit potentials: large amplitude (6-8 mV), long duration, polyphasic. Reduced recruitment pattern with rapid firing of few units.

Right and left first dorsal interosseous, abductor pollicis brevis, extensor digitorum communis: fibrillations +1 to +2, positive sharp waves +1. Large amplitude MUPs with reduced recruitment. Fasciculation potentials present in biceps bilaterally.
T6-T8 paraspinal muscles: fibrillations +1 bilaterally. Sparse fasciculation potentials. Abnormal MUP morphology.
Right tibialis anterior: sparse fibrillations, positive sharp waves. Gastrocnemius: fasciculation potentials. Recruitment mildly reduced. Changes less prominent than upper body.

Median motor: CMAP amplitude 4.8 mV right, 3.9 mV left (mildly reduced); distal latency and conduction velocity normal. Ulnar motor: CMAP amplitude 3.2 mV left (reduced); conduction velocity 52 m/s (normal). Peroneal motor: CMAP amplitude 3.1 mV right (mildly reduced); conduction velocity 44 m/s. No conduction block identified.

Median sensory: SNAP amplitude 22 uV right, 20 uV left — NORMAL. Ulnar sensory: SNAP amplitude 15 uV right — NORMAL. Sural sensory: SNAP amplitude 18 uV right — NORMAL. All sensory conduction velocities within normal limits.

specialized_test.impression: Active denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation (large amplitude, long duration, polyphasic MUPs, reduced recruitment) are present in the bulbar, cervical, and thoracic body regions, with early lumbosacral involvement. Sensory nerve conduction studies are normal. No conduction block identified. Findings indicate a widespread anterior horn cell process involving multiple body regions with preserved sensory function

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. H is a 62-year-old right-handed woman who presents for neurological evaluation of an 8-month history of progressive dysarthria, dysphagia, and limb weakness. She initially noticed that her speech was becoming slurred and quieter approximately 8 months ago, which she initially attributed to fatigue after a long day teaching. Over the following months, her speech worsened and she began having difficulty swallowing solid foods, requiring her to cut food into smaller pieces. She has had several episodes of coughing and choking while eating, particularly with thin liquids. Her husband noted that her voice has taken on a nasal quality and that she occasionally has uncontrollable laughing or crying that seems out of proportion to the situation.

Approximately 6 months ago, she noticed progressive bilateral arm weakness, initially affecting her left hand more than her right. She has difficulty buttoning shirts, opening jars, and holding a pen for extended periods. Over the past 3-4 months, she has also noticed bilateral leg weakness with difficulty climbing stairs and rising from low chairs. She denies any sensory symptoms, bladder or bowel dysfunction, or diplopia. She has noticed twitching in her tongue and arms.

Her primary care physician ordered cervical spine MRI which showed moderate spondylosis. The question of cervical myelopathy as the etiology of her symptoms has been raised, though the bulbar symptoms are not easily explained by cervical disease alone. She has no significant family history of neurodegenerative disease and no toxic exposures. Review of systems is otherwise negative.
